newsitem.title: USA: GM averts one strike, faces another deadline.
newsitem.headline: GM averts one strike, faces another deadline.

text.p: General Motors Corp., which averted a strike early Saturday at its Cadillac assembly plant, faces another strike deadline by the United Auto Workers, this time at a key transmission plant.
Officials of UAW Local 735 at the GM Hydramatic plant in Ypsilanti, Mich., confirmed on Sunday that they set a strike deadline of 11:59 p.m. EDT Friday, Aug. 15.

The plant, part of the Willow Run complex that built B-24 bombers during World War II, employs about 5,900 people and makes rear-wheel-drive transmissions and components for transmissions built elsewhere.

A prolonged walkout at the plant could force GM to shut down a number of North American powertrain and assembly plants. A six-day strike in July at GM's Warren, Mich., transmission plant resulted in the idling of six assembly lines and more than 17,000 workers.

GM has suffered six strikes so far this year and has averted several more threatened walkouts as it tangled with the UAW over staffing levels and outside contracting at about 120 U.S. assembly and parts plants. Nearly a year after GM signed a national agreement, it still has eight U.S. facilities without local labour agreements.
Early Saturday morning, GM and UAW Local 22 reached a tentative contract deal that averted a threatened strike at GM's Cadillac assembly plant here.
A ratification vote by the local's 3,600 members has not been scheduled yet. But Local 22 President Ed Ptasznik said Sunday that workers were told to report to work on their regular shifts on Monday.
The plant in the Hamtramck, Mich., enclave in Detroit produces the Cadillac Seville, DeVille and Eldorado models. The deal is expected to keep GM's launch of its new 1998 Seville on track.
"The bargaining committee was satisfied with the commitments that they got," Ptasznik said.

A prolonged walkout could have disrputed GM's ambitious launch plans for the '98 Seville, which it aims to position as a world class luxury car that can compete head-to-head with Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Lexus. GM will unveil the car next month in the German automakers' backyard, at the international auto show in Frankfurt, Germany.
Details about the Local 22 settlement were not disclosed because workers had not yet been briefed on the deal.
But in nearly every local settlement this year, GM has agreed to add jobs to meet UAW demands for replacements of retiring workers to ease a growing workload
GM has tried to resist such demands, maintaining that it needs to shrink its work force to become competitive with Ford Motor Co., Chrysler Corp., and Japanese automakers.

Among locals that still have not reached agreement with the automaker is one at two brake plants in Dayton, Ohio, that struck in March 1996 for 17 days, forcing GM to shut down 26 of 29 North American assembly plants, idling more than 175,000 workers and costing the automaker $900 million in lost profits.
During the second quarter, GM said its profits were reduced by $490 million because of strikes in Oklahoma City, and Pontiac, Mich.
